hypotheses.justification: The proof uses hV only to build `hF` for `supCode_le_iff`, which gives the inclusion `supCode c {V,W} ⊆ U`. That inclusion holds without it. Here `supCode c F = regular c (⋃₀ F)`, and `mem_regular` says `p ∈ regular c X ↔ p ∈ c ∧ ∀ q ∈ c, p ⊆ q → ∃ r ∈ X, q ⊆ r`. If p ∈ supCode c {V,W}, then p ∈ c, and every q ∈ c with p ⊆ q has some r ∈ V ∪ W with q ⊆ r. Since `Partition` gives V ⊆ U (h.1) and W ⊆ U (h.2.1), this r is in U. So p ∈ regular c U by `mem_regular`, and `regular c U = U` by hU.2. The reverse inclusion (rest of the proof) already uses only hU.1, `code_lower c U hU` and the last clause of `Partition`; it never touches hV or hW. So the theorem is still true and provable without hV. hW can also be dropped, separately or together with hV.

The argument is the same as for hV. hW is used only in `hF`, which feeds `supCode_le_iff` to get `supCode c {V,W} ⊆ U`. Instead, unfold `supCode` to `regular c (⋃₀ {V,W})` and use `mem_regular`. Any witness r ∈ V ∪ W lies in U, because `Partition` gives V ⊆ U and W ⊆ U. Hence p ∈ regular c U, and `regular c U = U` by hU.2. The reverse inclusion uses only hU (`hU.1`, `code_lower c U hU`) and the covering clause of `Partition`. Both hV and hW can be removed at once.
